hints: Notice the total resistance is $R + r$, so it changes from $10 + 0.5 = 10.5\ \Omega$ to $20 + 0.5 = 20.5\ \Omega$.
Connect this to current using $I = E/(R+r)$ and ask whether the denominator exactly doubles when $R$ doubles.
Then compare lost volts $Ir$ and terminal p.d. $V = E - Ir$, and power $P = I^2R$, for the smaller current with the larger $R$.
walkthrough: Write the current from e.m.f. $E$, external resistance $R$ and internal resistance $r = 0.5\ \Omega$ as $I = E/(R + r)$.
Initially $R + r = 10 + 0.5 = 10.5\ \Omega$ and finally $R + r = 20 + 0.5 = 20.5\ \Omega$, with $E$ unchanged because e.m.f. is a property of the cell.
Hence $I$ changes in the ratio $10.5/20.5$, which is slightly greater than $0.5$, so the current decreases but does not exactly halve.
The power in the external resistor $P = I^2R$ decreases because $I^2$ falls by almost a factor of four while $R$ only doubles.
The terminal p.d. $V = E - Ir$ increases because $I$ is smaller, so the lost volts $Ir$ across the internal resistance is smaller.
Therefore the claim that the current will halve is the statement that is not correct. This is option A

options.A: Total resistance changes from $10.5\ \Omega$ to $20.5\ \Omega$, which is not a doubling, so $I = E/(R+r)$ falls by slightly less than half.
options.B: The e.m.f. depends only on the cell itself, so changing the external $10\ \Omega$ to $20\ \Omega$ leaves it unchanged.
options.C: With $P = I^2R$, the fall in current dominates the rise in $R$, so power in the external resistor decreases.
options.D: Terminal p.d. $V = E - Ir$ rises because the smaller current gives a smaller lost volts $Ir$ across the $0.5\ \Omega$ internal resistance.
